posts.title: Why every learner starts in the yard
posts.excerpt: Behind the depot there is a fenced square of old asphalt with faded white bays. Every one of our learners begins there, and some stay longer than others.
posts.content:
Behind the depot there is a fenced square of old asphalt with faded white bays. Every one of our learners begins there, and some stay longer than others.

No traffic, no audience

The yard has one great quality: nothing happens in it unless you make it happen. Nobody is behind you, nobody is waiting at the junction and nobody is watching from the pavement. That leaves your whole attention for the things that matter in the first hour: where your hands go, how the clutch bites, how gently a car can stop.

Tomas, who founded the school, used to say that a learner who has stopped a car smoothly fifty times will stop it smoothly on Market Street without thinking. Forty years later we still find that he was right.

How long it takes

Most people leave the yard during their second lesson. Some leave in the first twenty minutes. A few stay for five lessons, and those learners are often the calmest drivers we have ever sent to test. Nobody leaves until they ask to.

posts.title: Three mirror habits that stick
posts.excerpt: Examiners mark more faults for mirrors than for anything else. Here are the three habits Mara teaches in the first week, and why they last.
posts.content:
Examiners mark more faults for mirrors than for anything else. Here are the three habits Mara teaches in the first week, and why they last.

Before every signal

Mirror, then signal, never the other way round. You are telling the road what you are about to do, so you should know who is listening first. We say it out loud for the first few lessons until it becomes boring.

Before every change of speed

Slowing down for a junction is a change other drivers need to know about. A glance in the centre mirror before you brake takes half a second and tells you whether the car behind is close enough to matter.

When nothing is happening

On a quiet stretch of the ring road, look in the mirror every few seconds anyway. It keeps a picture of the road behind you in your head, so that when you do need it, you already have it.

posts.title: What examiners look for at a roundabout
posts.excerpt: Coldwell has five exits and a reputation. Daniel explains what the examiner is really watching for, and why stopping is not always the safe choice.
posts.content:
Coldwell has five exits and a reputation. Daniel explains what the examiner is really watching for, and why stopping is not always the safe choice.

Planning, early

Most roundabout faults happen fifty metres before the roundabout. Read the sign, choose your lane, check your mirror and signal while there is still plenty of time. If the approach is calm, the roundabout itself usually is too.

Reading the gap

Examiners mark learners who stop when the way is clear almost as often as learners who go when it is not. We practise judging the gap from the left until it feels ordinary, at quiet hours first and at busy ones later.

Leaving well

Signal left as you pass the exit before yours, check your nearside mirror and leave in the lane you entered. It sounds like a lot. After six lessons on Coldwell it will feel like one movement.

posts.title: Driving in the first frost
posts.excerpt: The first frosty morning of the year always brings a few nervous telephone calls. Here is what we do differently on the moor road when the temperature drops.
posts.content:
The first frosty morning of the year always brings a few nervous telephone calls. Here is what we do differently on the moor road when the temperature drops.

Clear every window

A small hole scraped in the windscreen is not enough. We clear every window and the mirrors before the car moves, and we leave five minutes earlier so nobody is tempted to hurry.

Gentle everything

On frost, the car needs gentle inputs: gentle on the accelerator, gentle with the steering, and braking early and softly. We use a higher gear when moving off on a slope so the wheels are less likely to spin.

Where frost hides

Shade under the trees on Mill Lane, the bridge over the river and the north side of the moor road stay icy long after the sun is up. We point them out on every winter lesson, so learners start to see them for themselves.

posts.title: A morning on the Harrow Moor road
posts.excerpt: Single track, passing places, sheep and a long downhill: why the moor road is the lesson our learners remember longest.
posts.content:
Single track, passing places, sheep and a long downhill: why the moor road is the lesson our learners remember longest.

Passing places

On a single-track road the rule is simple: whoever is nearer a passing place pulls in. Learning to look far enough ahead to see the other car, and decide early, is one of the best lessons in planning we know.

The long downhill

From the cattle grid to the river the road drops steadily for two miles. We use a lower gear, keep a steady speed and let the engine do the work. It teaches more about speed control than any amount of town driving.

Why we go

There is a lay-by at the top with a view across three valleys. Almost every learner stops there for a minute on their first moor lesson, and almost every one of them says the same thing: that driving might, after all, be a pleasure.

posts.title: Thursday theory evenings are back
posts.excerpt: Tea, hazard-perception clips and honest answers, upstairs at the depot every Thursday at seven. Free for our learners and their parents.
posts.content:
Tea, hazard-perception clips and honest answers, upstairs at the depot every Thursday at seven. Free for our learners and their parents.

What happens

Ellen started the theory evenings in 1986 with a blackboard and a teapot. We still use the teapot. Each week an instructor takes one subject, such as stopping distances, motorway rules or the hazard-perception test, and we finish with questions from the room.

Who comes

Learners at every stage, parents who supervise practice drives, and a few people who passed years ago and want to check their habits. The room holds twenty, so please tell Joan if you are coming.

This term

September is road signs and markings, October is the hazard-perception test, and November is driving in the dark and the rain, with Sam.
